                                         Figure 1. Comprehensive comparison of our MaTVLM. (a) Performance comparison across multiple benchmarks. Our
                                         MaTVLM achieves competitive results with the teacher model TinyLLaVA, surpassing existing VLMs with similar parameter scales,
                                         as well as Mamba-based VLMs. (b) Speed Comparison of Token Throughput. Tokens generated per second for different token lengths.
                                         Our MaTVLM achieves a 3.6× speedup compared to the teacher model TinyLLaVA. (c) GPU Memory Usage Comparison. A detailed
                                         comparison of memory usage during inference for different token lengths, highlighting the optimization advantages with a 27.5% reduction
                                         in usage for our MaTVLM over TinyLLaVA.

2.2. Structured State Space Models
                                                                Large vision-language models (VLMs) process longer se-
Structured state space models (S4) [17, 23, 24, 26, 42, 45]     quences than LLMs, resulting in slower training and
scale efficiently in a linear manner with sequence length.      inference. As previously mentioned, Mamba-2 archi-
Mamba[23] introduces selective SSMs, while Mamba-               tecture exhibits linear scaling and offers significantly
2 [17] refines this by linking SSMs to attention variants,      higher efficiency compared to transformer. To leverage
achieving 2–8× speedup and performance comparable to            these advantages, we propose a hybrid VLM architecture
transformers. Mamba-based VLMs [29, 43, 63, 69] pri-            MaTVLM that integrates Mamba-2 and transformer com-
marily replace the transformer-based large language mod-        ponents, aiming to balance computational efficiency with
els (LLMs) entirely with the pre-trained Mamba-2 language       optimal performance.
model, achieving both competitive performance and en-
hanced computational efficiency.                                3.1. Mamba Preliminaries

Figure 2. The proposed MaTVLM integrates both Mamba-2 and transformer components. The model consists of a vision encoder, a
connector, and a language model same as the base VLM. The language model is composed of both transformer decoder layers and Mamba-
2 decoder layers, where Mamba-2 layers replace only attention in transformer layers, while the other components remain unchanged. The
model is trained using a knowledge distillation approach, incorporating probability distribution and layer-wise distillation loss. During the
distillation training, only Mamba-2 layers and the connector are trainable, while transformer layers remain fixed.

vestigate the impact of Mamba-2 layer placement on the               Despite its advantages, MaTVLM has several limita-
performance. Specifically, we replace the transformer de-            tions. While initializing Mamba-2 with pre-trained atten-
coder layers with Mamba-2 layers in four configurations:             tion weights aids convergence, it may not fully leverage
all at the beginning, all in the middle, all at the end, and         its implicit state representations. This could be improved
evenly distributed. Notably, the all-at-the-end configuration        through tailored initialization strategies, such as gradient
fails to enable effective distillation, resulting in incoher-        matching or an additional pretraining phase. Additionally,
ent responses. As shown in Tab. 3, the evenly distributed            due to the limited GPU resources available in this study, we

erage score, respectively. These results highlight the impor-        integration ratios and conduct hybrid experiments on larger
tance of evenly integrating Mamba-2 layers throughout the            VLMs to evaluate scalability and performance. Address-
model to optimize performance.                                       ing these challenges will further improve the efficiency and
